title: Job 19:23–29
context: Job continues. He longs for his words to be written permanently (19:23–24), then declares, “I know that my Redeemer lives” (19:25), and hopes to see God on his side (19:26–27), before warning the friends of judgment (19:28–29). The word rendered “Redeemer” is used elsewhere of a family member who defends or restores a relative (Leviticus 25:25; Ruth 4). Readers have taken 19:25–27 as hope of a vindicator in this life, a vindicator after Job’s death, a resurrection hope, or a pointer to Christ; how far the language already speaks of resurrection, or of a vindicator standing on the earth in Job’s own day, is debated, and no single reading is declared here. The Hebrew of 19:26 is difficult, and translations differ over whether Job expects to see God in his flesh or apart from it.

verses.text: “Oh that my words were now written! Oh that they were inscribed in a book!
verses.arminianNotes: “Oh that my words were now written! Oh that they were inscribed in a book!” Arminian readers see Job longing for a permanent record that will vindicate him beyond his lifetime.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a desire for lasting testimony. Many readers in both traditions notice the irony that Job’s words are in fact preserved in Scripture.

verses.text: That with an iron pen and lead they were engraved in the rock forever!
verses.arminianNotes: “That with an iron pen and lead they were engraved in the rock forever!” Arminian readers see Job wishing for an enduring inscription, stressing his confidence that he will be proven right.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the image of permanent engraving. The exact method described is uncertain, but readers in this tradition see the point as Job’s desire for a witness that cannot be erased.

verses.text: But as for me, I know that my Redeemer lives. In the end, he will stand upon the earth.
verses.arminianNotes: “But as for me, I know that my Redeemer lives. In the end, he will stand upon the earth.” Many Arminian readers hear Christ here, while others read a vindicator in this life or after death.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hold several readings: a vindicator within Job’s lifetime, after his death, a resurrection hope, and the Christological reading common in Christian worship. Readers in this tradition commonly hear real hope without settling every exegetical question.

verses.text: After my skin is destroyed, then I will see God in my flesh,
verses.arminianNotes: “After my skin is destroyed, then I will see God in my flesh,” Arminian readers often hear resurrection hope here, while acknowledging that the Hebrew is difficult and that some read a hope of seeing God after death.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the difficulty of the Hebrew. Some read a bodily resurrection hope, others a vindication seen before death, and others a vision of God after death; readers in this tradition hold these options with care.

verses.text: whom I, even I, will see on my side. My eyes will see, and not as a stranger. “My heart is consumed within me.
verses.arminianNotes: “… whom I, even I, will see on my side. My eyes will see, and not as a stranger.” Arminian readers see Job’s personal longing to see God with his own eyes as friend, not foe.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a personal hope of seeing God favorably. Readers in this tradition note the contrast with Job’s earlier sense of God as an enemy, and they hear a deep longing for fellowship.

verses.text: If you say, ‘How we will persecute him!’ because the root of the matter is found in me,
verses.arminianNotes: “If you say, ‘How we will persecute him!’ because the root of the matter is found in me.” Arminian readers see Job warning the friends against continuing to treat him as guilty.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Job turning to warn the friends. The verse is difficult, but readers in this tradition commonly take it as rejecting the friends’ claim that the cause of his trouble lies in him.

verses.text: be afraid of the sword, for wrath brings the punishments of the sword, that you may know there is a judgment.”
verses.arminianNotes: “… be afraid of the sword, for wrath brings the punishments of the sword, that you may know there is a judgment.” Arminian readers see Job warning that God will judge false accusers.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Job appealing to a coming judgment. The book later vindicates Job’s warning when the LORD rebukes the friends (42:7), and readers in this tradition see justice ultimately belonging to God.
